action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_scrape
tools.description: Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state. `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call. Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state. `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call. Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_search
tools.description: Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application. Finder is an application like any other: clicking the desktop, the Dock, or a Finder window (including Go to Folder) requires a Finder grant. The menu bar does not, as long as the app that is frontmost is one you already have access to.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. ## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

1	# Atomization brief (shared by every Flint ingest agent)
2	
3	Read this whole file before writing anything. It holds the rules the Harries review taught (2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes). The review gate will check every rule here.
4	
5	## Schema
6	
7	Follow `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ingest-book\SKILL.md` exactly: `_domain.md`, `_book.md` (map and resume checkpoint, updated after EACH chapter or unit), and entries named `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md` with kind one of principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim. Use the frontmatter keys exactly as the skill gives them. The body has **What it is** / **Why it works** / **When to apply** / **When NOT to apply** (mandatory, non-trivial) / **Example** / **Related**.
8	
9	Style reference, read before writing: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer\case-study--isometric-sprinter-and-hurdler.md`, plus one principle file in the same folder.
10	
11	## Voices: label every one
12	
13	- **The source author's statements are plain text.**
14	- **Eric's views** (from `docs/method-baseline.md` or his reviews) are prefixed "Eric's baseline:" or "Eric's review:".
15	- **Your own reasoning, application or synthesis** is prefixed "Inference:".
16	- **Nothing unlabeled that the author did not say.** The most common failures: a judgment from Eric's review written as if the author said it; a mechanism the author never gave presented as "why it works" (write "The author gives no mechanism. Inference: ..."); an invented example.
17	
18	## Lessons from the Supertraining Chapter 1 review (2026-09-26: 30 FIX, 1 NO-GO of 41)
19	
20	- **Keep the source's internal contradictions.** When a book says X on one page and not-X on another, record both with their pages and set `contested`. Never pick one side silently. The NO-GO entry reversed the book's SJ-CMJ strength-deficit rule because the book states it both ways.
21	- **Name the right voice.** In co-authored books, write "the authors" unless a passage clearly belongs to one author. A passage that names Verkhoshansky in the third person is Siff writing.
22	- **Keep `proven` rare and scoped.** Scope it to the replicated core (for example, "Hill's force-velocity curve"), never the whole entry, and mark any disputed sentence inside it. Four of eight `proven` ratings were lowered.
23	- **No mechanism the source does not give.** About a dozen "Why it works" sections supplied physiology the book never states. Label it "Inference:" or leave it out.
24	- **Do not add "well established" or "modern research shows" without a citation.** Name the paper, or delete the phrase.
25	
26	## Lessons from the 2026-09-27 review wave (Supertraining Ch2-3, Issurin Ch3, Bondarchuk, Evans, Old Bull)
27	
28	- **Invented Examples are the most common failure.** 34 of 36 Supertraining Ch2-3a Examples were unlabelled inventions. Use the source's own example where it gives one; otherwise start the Example with "Inference:".
29	- **"Verified against the page image" means you opened the image.** Four Issurin Ch3 entries claimed it for figures they had misread (Fig 3.7 inverted, a Table 3.7 row swapped). Sparse slides are not "bare diagrams" until you have looked.
30	- **Name the population and method the source gives.** Bondarchuk's data are 7,000+ native and foreign athletes, questionnaires, r >= 0.349, steroid-free; entries that said "Soviet athletes" were wrong everywhere.
31	- **Check what a cited paper actually says.** Issurin 2016's critique targets Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional model, not Issurin's A-T-R; Herzog & Leonard 2000 shows force enhancement, against the book's sentence. When the book misreports a study, record both.
32	- **No review history in entries.** "Prior version", "corrected from a NO-GO finding" and similar belong in `staging/fixes_*_applied.md`, never in the entry body.
33	- **Fix logs must match the files.** One fixer log claimed fixes that were not made. Fixers run their own grep checks and paste the output.
34	- **Section headers use the vault form** `**What it is** —` (with the em dash). Do not add suffixes such as ": mandatory". Em dashes are banned only in titles and body text. Never wrap a `[[wikilink]]` across lines.
35	
36	## Evidence
37	
38	- Every number, definition and quote carries a checkable locator: PDF page (and printed page if it differs), or file plus timestamp. Never write "confirmed in PDF" unless you opened that page.
39	- Never invent a number. Keep ambiguity visible: mark unclear audio or OCR as unclear, and do not harmonize two conflicting numbers from the source; record both with their locators.
40	- OCR sources (`staging/ocr/*.md`): pages listed as low_confidence in the header must be checked against the page image before any number from them is cited. Use the Read tool on the PDF page, or render it.
41	- **OCR confidence scores miss the worst errors** (checked 2026-09-27). Zatsiorsky 2e: the OCR interleaves the two columns and the sidebars line by line, so its text is not readable prose; use it only to find content, and read and quote from the page image. *CFTS*: single-column prose that mostly reads in order, but upside-down lines come out as gibberish, some lines are dropped, and figures are scrambled, all at "0 low-confidence pages". For any OCR source, quote only after checking the page image, and read every figure and table from the image.
42	
43	## Confidence
44	
45	- Practitioner courses and lectures: ceiling `supported`.
46	- Books: `proven` only for established, widely replicated physiology or mechanics. Soviet-era or single-lab empirical findings and training prescriptions: `supported` at most. `untested` for single cases and anecdotes. `contested` where another library source or modern evidence disagrees (say which).
47	
48	## Dedup and converge
49	
50	Before each entry, grep `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library` and the staging library (`C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\staging\library`) for the concept. If it is covered, add a new entry only for a genuinely new angle, and link the existing one in Related. List reciprocal-link suggestions in your final report. Never edit files in the vault or another agent's staging folder.
51	
52	## Baylor context
53	
54	Read `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\docs\method-baseline.md` (approved). Use it in When to apply, labelled "Eric's baseline:". Department names: Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, Applied Performance. Plain style, no em dashes. Use commas, colons and parentheses.
55	
56	## Scope and output
57	
58	- Write ONLY into your assigned staging folder. No git, no vault edits.
59	- Stop at a chapter or unit boundary. It is better to finish fewer chapters well; the `_book.md` checkpoint lets the next batch resume.
60	- Final reply: entries by kind and by confidence; chapters or units done and pending with page ranges; reciprocal-link suggestions; unclear or contradictory spots in the source; anything you could not read.
61

1	---
2	name: ingest-book
3	description: >-
4	  Ingest a book (PDF/EPUB full-text, Kindle highlights, or framework-only from a
5	  physical book) into the SecondBrain library as atomized, citable advisor entries. Use
6	  when the user wants to "ingest a book", "add a book to my library/advisors",
7	  "/ingest-book", or points at a book file for the advisor system. Do not use for
8	  articles, transcripts, or general resources (use ingest-resource).
9	argument-hint: "[book file or title] [domain]"
10	---
11	
12	# Ingest Book
13	
14	Turn a book into atomized, citable entries under the library subtree, grouped by domain and book, ready for the `advisor` skill.
15	
16	**Library root:** `vault_library` in the selected platform config
17	**Paths:** canonical vault locations live in `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.<platform>.json` (`vault_library`, `vault_root`) — load it if unsure; if a literal path here ever disagrees, the config wins.
18	**Extractors:** `~/.claude/skills/ingest-book/lib/extract_epub.py`, `extract_pdf.py`
19	Run extractors inside the context-mode sandbox (`ctx_execute`, language python) so raw book text never enters the conversation — only the atomized entries you write do.
20	
21	## Model split (cost vs quality)
22	
23	This skill mixes three kinds of work with very different model needs:
24	- **Extraction & structure mapping** (probe, chapter map, text cleanup) — deterministic
25	  Python in the sandbox. **Zero model tokens; model choice irrelevant.**
26	- **Orchestration** (searches, `_book.md` updates, dedup checks) — mechanical.
27	  **Haiku-tier is fine.**
28	- **Atomization** (Phase 2/3: distilling prose into accurate entries with correct
29	  mechanism-vs-claim, honest confidence, and a real "when NOT to apply") — this is where
30	  the advisor's entire value is created. **Run on Sonnet or stronger. Do NOT use Haiku
31	  for atomization** — a weak distillation becomes a permanent low-quality entry, and the
32	  generated output is only ~3K tokens/chapter, so quality-per-token matters far more than
33	  price-per-token. Cost levers that DON'T hurt quality: atomize only chapters you'll
34	  consult, and checkpoint + `/clear` between chapter batches (see Rules) so context
35	  doesn't compound across the book.
36	
37	## Schema for every entry note
38	
39	Filename: `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md`, `kind ∈ {principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim}`.
40	
41	```yaml
42	---
43	type: library-entry
44	kind: principle
45	domain: <domain-slug>
46	book: <book-slug>
47	chapter: "N"            # or section label; "" if highlights with no location
48	topic: <2-5 word topic>
49	category: [tag, tag]
50	confidence: proven      # proven | supported | untested | contested
51	ingest-tier: full-text  # full-text | highlights | framework-only
52	created: <YYYY-MM-DD>
53	---
54	
55	# <Human title of the idea>
56	
57	**What it is** — one tight paragraph.
58	**Why it works** — mechanism, not restatement.
59	**When to apply** — concrete triggers.
60	**When NOT to apply** — scope limits. (MANDATORY — never omit.)
61	**Example** — one concrete instance.
62	```
63	
64	**Confidence is bounded by tier:** full-text ≤ proven; highlights ≤ supported;
65	framework-only ≤ untested. Set `contested` by hand when sources conflict.
66	
67	## Phase 1 — Intake
68	
69	1. Identify: book title, author, source type (PDF/EPUB | Kindle highlights | physical), target domain.
70	2. Compute `<book-slug>` = `kebab(title)--kebab(lastname)` (e.g. `supertraining--verkhoshansky`).
71	3. If the domain folder/`_domain.md` doesn't exist, create them (mirror the S&C `_domain.md` format).
72	4. Build `_book.md` chapter map:
73	   - EPUB/PDF: run the extractor with `--list` / `--probe` to get the chapter or page structure.
74	   - Physical: ask the user for the chapter list, or assemble from a verified public listing.
75	   Write `_book.md` (template below) with every chapter `status: pending`.
76	
77	`_book.md` template:
78	```markdown
79	---
80	type: book-index
81	book: <book-slug>
82	title: <full title>
83	author: <author>
84	domain: <domain-slug>
85	ingest-tier: full-text | highlights | framework-only
86	source: "<file path or 'physical' or 'kindle-highlights'>"
87	created: <YYYY-MM-DD>
88	---
89	
90	# <title> — ingest map
91	
92	| # | Chapter | Status | Entries |
93	|---|---------|--------|---------|
94	| 0 | <title> | pending | 0 |
95	```
96	
97	## Phase 2 — Extract (by tier)
98	
99	**Full-text (PDF/EPUB):**
100	- First run `extract_pdf.py --probe`. If `scanned: true`, STOP the full-text path:
101	  tell the user the PDF is image-only, and fall back to framework-only tier (set
102	  `ingest-tier: framework-only`, cap confidence at untested). Never emit full-text-
103	  confidence entries from a scanned file.
104	- Work **one chapter at a time** (EPUB `--chapter N`; PDF `--pages A-B`, where A and B are
105	  0-based PDF indexes and the range is inclusive: `--pages 12-20` returns 9 pages). Each page
106	  comes back with `page` (0-based index) and `viewer_page` (what a PDF viewer shows, index + 1).
107	  Cite pages one way throughout a book and state the convention in `_book.md`. For each:
108	  extract candidate ideas → atomize per the schema → write entry notes.
109	- **After each chapter**, update that row in `_book.md` to `status: done` with the
110	  entry count. This is the resume checkpoint — never batch this update.
111	
112	**Kindle highlights:**
113	- Parse `My Clippings.txt` or the highlights export in the sandbox. Cluster highlights
114	  by theme; write one entry per theme. `ingest-tier: highlights`, confidence ≤ supported.
115	- Attribute `chapter` from the highlight's location metadata when present, else "".
116	
117	**Framework-only (physical / scanned):**
118	- Briefly interview the user for their takeaways. Supplement with *verified* public
119	  chapter summaries. Write 5–15 framework-level entries. `ingest-tier: framework-only`,
120	  confidence ≤ untested.
121	
122	## Phase 3 — Quality gate (run before writing each batch)
123	
124	- One idea per note. If an extracted point is compound, split it.
125	- "When NOT to apply" present and non-trivial.
126	- **Dedup + converge:** before writing, `memsearch search` the library for the same
127	  concept. If an existing entry (any book) covers it, DON'T duplicate — instead add a
128	  `[[wikilink]]` + one line to both notes recording the agreement, and only add a new
129	  note if it contributes a genuinely new angle.
130	- Never overwrite an existing file; on slug collision append `-2`.
131	
132	## Phase 4 — Close-out
133	
134	1. Set all done rows in `_book.md`; if partial, leave pending rows for next session.
135	2. Add the book to `_domain.md`'s `books:` list and the "Books in this domain" section.
136	3. Add the book-slug to the advisor persona's `books:` list (`advisors/<domain>.md`)
137	   if an advisor exists.
138	4. Run `memsearch index "<vault_library>"` using the selected platform config
139	   so entries are searchable immediately (don't wait for the SessionEnd hook).
140	5. Commit the vault using `vault_root` from the selected platform config: `git -C "<vault_root>" add Knowledge/library && git commit -m "ingest(<book-slug>): <N> entries, ch X-Y"`.
141	6. Report: entries by kind and confidence, links created, chapters remaining.
142	
143	## Rules
144	- Raw book text stays in the sandbox; only atomized entries enter context/the vault.
145	- Resumable by design: `_book.md` is the source of truth for "where am I".
146	- A 300-page book is a multi-session job — stop at a chapter boundary, never mid-chapter.
147

1	# Eric's method baseline (draft for Eric's review)
2	
3	Purpose: this is the step-1 baseline for Flint. It pulls every position, practice, and decision rule out of Eric's own 23-document corpus (Baylor Applied Performance playbook, protocols, assessment manual, professional writing, and HHPR 5355 graduate-course material) so that every future synthesis note comparing an outside source (Landon Evans, TB's Training Info, Old Bull, Harries RTP, SCN/Moyer, etc.) has something of Eric's own to compare against. Date: 2026-09-26. Revised 2026-09-28 with Eric's method interview (`docs/interview/2026-09-28-method-interview.md`, 30 of 30 answered).
4	
5	## Provenance note (read this before the bullets)
6	
7	Not all 23 documents are Eric's own words, and the two richest sources (the class transcripts) have a diarization problem. Read this once, then use these tags:
8	
9	- **Eric-authored, high confidence**: the two SportSmith articles, the Performance Playbook Development Plan, the Force Plate Testing V3 and Iso Seated Calf protocols, the Applied Performance Playbook (departmental document under his unit), and the HD ODSF metrics note (adopted practice, though the framework itself is Hawkin Dynamics' own).
10	- **Course slide decks (Week 1, Week 3, Class 4)**: co-branded to Ruf/Rash/Wenger on every title slide. Per `spring-2026-teaching.md`, Eric was the assigned instructor for the Feb. 5 and Feb. 12 sessions (Week 3 Lecture and Class 4 2026 respectively), so bullets from those two decks are marked **Explicit**. Week 1 (Jan. 22, "All") and Class 8/Lesson 8 (Mar. 19, Wenger's session) are marked **Inferred** — shared team material, not confirmed as Eric's individual position.
11	- **Both class transcripts (Class 1, Class 3) are diarized entirely under one Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line, across 100+ minutes combined.** This is true even for Class 3 (Feb. 5), which the syllabus assigns solo to Rash. Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name rather than doing real per-speaker diarization. That means specific sentences in these transcripts cannot be confidently attributed to Rash vs. Ruf vs. Wenger. Bullets drawn from the transcripts are marked **Inferred**, with a citation note, even where the statement itself is a direct, confident, first-person claim in the text. Flint should treat these as "the HHPR 5355 teaching team's shared position, individual speaker unconfirmed" until Eric ratifies them.
12	  - **Confirmed by Eric, 2026-09-26:** HHPR 5355 is taught each spring by Chris Ruf, Eric and Mike Wenger. The lecture material is split among the three of them. This confirms the course is partly Eric's, but it cannot say who spoke a given transcript line. So transcript bullets stay tagged Inferred and read as **course team positions**. Each one becomes Eric's own only when he claims it, in review or in the interview.
13	- **Reference material, not Eric's position**: `intencurriculumn.md` is Jason Avedesian's (Clemson) authored curriculum end to end, used by the Development Plan as a benchmark, not as something Eric wrote or necessarily agrees with. The two Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are explicitly staff templates filled in (thinly) by Geyer and Skodinski, not Eric. The AP Assessment Manual V12 and the TechnologyTemplateSOP (TMG) have uncertain/likely-legacy authorship (see Tensions below) and are marked accordingly.
14	
15	Sections below use **Explicit** (the source states Eric holds this position, with confidence in authorship per the tiers above) and **Inferred** (implied by protocol design, shared course material, or transcript content with unconfirmed speaker attribution).
16	
17	Tags added 2026-09-28 from the method interview:
18	
19	- **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Qn)**: Eric stated or claimed the position in the interview. His words are quoted as "Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Qn):". Q1 claimed exactly four course positions (Vermeil hierarchy, undulating periodization, Dynamic Correspondence, the football energy-system priority stack); other course material stays Inferred.
20	- **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Qn)**: Eric said the source or practice is not current. The old content is kept and marked, not deleted, so a synthesis note can see what changed.
21	- **Superseded by interview (Qn)**: a documented position, sometimes from Eric's own slides, that his interview answer replaces.
22	
23	---
24	
25	## Philosophy and decision principles
26	
27	- Applied Performance's stated mission is to "drive elite performance ... by leveraging science and technology through education and relationships," enabling the high-performance team to answer questions, ask better questions, and discover new ones — not to hand down answers unilaterally. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
28	- The department's four operating principles are Athlete Monitoring and Analysis, Athlete Evaluation and Return-to-Performance, Performance Team Collaboration, and Research and Development. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
29	- Institutional framing: "Prepare Champions for Life" across four pillars (academic, athletic, social, spiritual), operationalized through six "One Standard, One Accord" principles. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.3-4]

14	# Case Study: An Elite Sprinter and a Hurdler on Run-Specific Isometrics
15	
16	**What it is** — Natera presents two athletes (~93:07–101:49).
17	
18	**Elite male sprinter.** He was a strong, "power-hungry" athlete: a good accelerator but poorly elastic, with a weak max velocity.
19	- **Baseline:** back squat about **2.65× BW**; isometric mid-thigh pull **5.78× BW**. It is unclear whether that was single- or double-leg; the pull came before Natera moved to iso squats. CMJ about **59–62 cm**.
20	- **GPP:** eccentric calf work, then hip ISO holds progressing to switches.
21	- **SPP:** ankle and hip ISO catches, plus "ISO stadium descents," a loaded, cyclical isometric step-down that comes after the continuum.
22	- **Loads cited:** ankle ISO catch "up to 160 kg" (the transcript says "leaving up to 160 kilo"), which is implausible against his own 60 kg example and needs verifying on video. Hip ISO catch about 35 kg.
23	- **Reported changes:** CMJ +3 cm; CMJ power (~6,000 W) +200–300 W; takeoff velocity up; **RSI** "improved significantly," which he calls the main win; shorter contact times at about 30–40 m; longer acceleration and higher max velocity (around 11 m/s).
24	
25	**Female 100 m hurdler.** She was coached by a Polish coach whose name the ASR renders "Peter Marazu ski" (name unverified), with Natera collaborating. Her times stagnated in 2016–2017. Run-specific isometrics (RSI) were added in 2018 through mid-2019 alongside "track training" and traditional squats, deadlifts and Olympic lifts. She used **holds and pushes only**, and progressed past targets such as a **2× BW ankle hold**. Afterwards her hurdle times and speed improved to "elite level." Her quote to a reporter: "I don't lift heavy weights. I just hold them."
26	
27	*(Every number is single-source ASR from slides; the before/after charts are visual only. Verify at ~95:05–100:58.)*
28	
29	**Why it works** — Natera's interpretation: isometrics raised reactive strength without extra plyometric volume, and position-specific strength carried over into running. Neither interpretation can be separated from other causes in these data.
30	
31	**When to apply** — Use the sprinter as a **profile template**, not as evidence: high max strength (squat ≥2.5× BW) plus a low RSI and poor max velocity is the athlete Natera would target. In football that is the big, strong accelerator (RB/LB type) whose drop-jump RSI on ForceDecks is low for his strength. Track RSI and single-leg iso push together to see whether one moves without the other.
32	
33	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** Each case is n = 1 with concurrent training: sprint coaching, traditional lifting, technical work and maturation. There is no control, and the selection is plainly of successes. The hurdler also had a new collaborating coach, "great coaching and great technical training," per Natera himself. Elsewhere (~34:19–35:15) he reports programs where RSI was "the only change," and he concedes that is "not exactly a controlled scientific experiment." Do not cite these cases as evidence that RSI improves sprint speed. The 160 kg ankle catch must not become a target.
34	
35	**Example** — Screening question for a strong but non-reactive athlete: "Is this athlete's RSI low relative to his iso push ×BW?" If yes, he fits the sprinter case, and Natera would add ankle switches and catches after an eccentric calf base.
36	
37	**Related** — [[principle--isometric-overload-for-upright-running]] — the rationale these cases are offered to illustrate.

 "description": "This paper presents an interference-aware causal inference framework for evaluating defensive performance in American football, utilizing player tracking data. We model all 22 players jointly with a multi-agent Transformer to estimate counterfactual Expected Points Saved (EPS) for individual defenders while explicitly accounting for coordination, substitution, and other violations of independence. Using doubly robust estimation, adversarial representation balancing, and Bayesian uncertainty quantification, we recover causal defensive value that traditional tackle-based and predictive models systematically miss. Extensive synthetic validation, sensitivity analyses, and real-game examples demonstrate that explicitly modeling defensive interdependence substantially reduces bias and reveals hidden contributions across positions.",
 "chapters": null,

## Summary

Ben Jenkins, a PhD candidate at Florida Atlantic University, presents a causal model for crediting defenders in American football. Traditional metrics credit only the tackler, and predictive models favor high-volume tacklers. His framework models all 22 players jointly with a transformer, estimates expected points saved for each defender by comparing expected points added with and without that defender's tackle, and uses propensity weighting and doubly robust estimation. On the first 9 weeks of a 2022 season it credits set-up defenders, ranks known top players better than supervised models, and aggregates to team results. He calls it a proof of concept.

## Key claims

- Football has a defensive attribution problem: on a 6-yard loss, traditional metrics credit only the tackler though several defenders contributed. [00:00] [00:31]
- Supervised models predict outcomes, mix correlation with causation, favor high-volume tacklers and struggle to separate skill from opportunity. [01:01] [01:31]
- Causal inference asks what would have happened without the defender; it isolates individual contributions and separates player from scheme better, but needs more assumptions and quality control and cannot be applied in every scenario. [01:31] [02:01]
- Defenders do not act independently, so the model covers coordination, interference (for example, a defensive end setting the edge so a linebacker can tackle) and substitution effects, which violate independence. [02:31] [03:01] [03:31]
- The framework, called expected points saved, treats a defender making the tackle as the treatment and expected points added as the outcome. [04:02] [04:33]
- It uses a transformer over all 22 players, a propensity score model, an outcome model and inverse propensity weighting. [04:33] [05:04] [05:35]
- On the example play, the tackler scores highest and four other defenders get positive credit, which the speaker says shows the model captures coordinated effort. [06:09]
- Aaron Donald's expected points saved is around 0.27. [06:40]
- The method ranks players who earned All-Pro or Pro Bowl honors better than supervised models. [07:09] [07:39]
- Mean individual values aggregate to team level and explain 41% of variance in tackle play outcomes. [07:39]
- On synthetic data the method shows higher R-squared and lower RMSE than independent models, and ranks non-rookie players better against salaries and Pro Bowl status. [08:40]
- 68% of plays show significant interference effects, and modeling them reduces bias. [08:40] [09:10]
- The speaker calls it the first multi-agent causal inference framework in professional football for defensive evaluation; it is a proof of concept using the first 9 weeks of the 2022 regular season. [09:10]
- Intended next steps are quarterback decision-making and defensive back evaluation; stated uses are player evaluation, contract decisions and defensive scheme optimization. [09:41] [10:11]

## Numbers and definitions

- Expected points saved: expected points added on the play when the defender does not make the tackle, minus expected points added when he does (as described). [04:02]
- Expected points added: the traditional NFL metric of how much the offense benefits on a play. [04:02]
- Treatment: a binary indicator that the defender made the tackle. [04:02]
- 6-yard loss: the example running play. [00:00]
- 0.27: Aaron Donald's expected points saved; the speaker says each of his tackles prevents about 0.27 expected points. The captions describe the orange and blue distributions inconsistently (which is tackle and which is no tackle). [06:40] [07:09]
- 41% of variance in tackle play outcomes explained at team level. [07:39] [08:10]
- 68% of plays with significant interference effects. [08:40] [09:41]
- 9 weeks: the data available ("first 9 weeks of the 2022 NFL regular season"). [09:10]
- Data source named: 2024 NFL Big Data Bowl tracking data. [00:31]
- R-squared, RMSE, rank correlations and salary comparisons: stated as better, with no values in the captions. [08:40]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Interference-aware causal framework with a multi-agent transformer over 22 players. [02:31] [04:33]
- A directed acyclic graph with features: each defender's position, speed and direction, ball carrier features, relational features, 10 teammates, opponents and game context. [04:33] [05:04]
- Propensity score model and outcome model, with inverse propensity weighting to make a pseudo-population; doubly robust estimation for protection against model misspecification. [05:04] [05:35] [09:41]
- Validation by synthetic data, team-level aggregation, Pro Bowl and All-Pro agreement and salary rank. [07:39] [08:40]

## Limits and open questions

- Proof of concept on 9 weeks of one season, as the speaker says. [09:10]
- The talk does not say how many plays per defender, how the propensity model is checked, or how the treatment is defined for players who do not tackle but get credit.
- The video description mentions adversarial representation balancing, Bayesian uncertainty, and sensitivity analyses; none is described in the captions.
- Validation uses synthetic data and honors; real causal effects are not observable, as the speaker notes. [08:10]
- Scheme and assignment are not in the data; a questioner raised blitzers versus droppers, and the speaker's partial answer is propensity weighting, with scheme data expected to improve estimates. [11:43] [12:43]
- Claims of being first and of better ranking are the author's own and come from a competition presentation.
- "Tackle" here is the treatment; the audience question about pass rush disruption is answered only in general terms. [11:13]

## Q&A

- Does it handle pass plays and disruption without a tackle, such as Aaron Donald in the backfield? Yes, he gets positive credit for forcing the ball carrier elsewhere or lowering the odds a pass is beneficial. [10:43] [11:13]
- How does scheme (a blitzing linebacker versus a dropping one) confound the metric, and how would a team use scheme data? Ongoing research on scheme and responsibility; propensity weighting up-weights a low-probability defender's tackle; scheme data would improve estimates. [11:43] [12:17] [12:43]

## Summary

Eager argues that football analytics has used its three data families (play-by-play, hand-charted data, and player tracking) mostly one at a time, and that combining them gives better player evaluation. He shows three cases from Pro Football Focus (PFF): an expected pressure rate for pass rushers, a "bite distance" measure for linebackers on play action, and a speed-adjusted receiver grade for deep routes. In each case the hand-charted grade supplies the target and tracking data supplies a measure that is steadier from year to year or tracks athletic testing. The Q&A covers second-order effects, trade-offs and model context.

## Key claims

- Football analytics has advanced from a few public writers to many data sources, but each source is mostly used alone, and combining them would improve player evaluation [01:33].
- PFF charts every NFL and college game by hand, producing player grades and event labels. The NFL's tracking data comes from chips in shoulder pads and the ball [02:08, 02:40].
- For pass rushers, PFF's charted pressure and win-rate data served as training targets, and tracking data supplied the predictors, in two models (pressure and win rate) [06:16].
- The most important predictor of a pressure was the defender's vertical distance covered in the first second. The model was an XGBoost ensemble of decision trees [06:47].
- Charted position labels (nose tackle, edge defender) also entered the model, so it carries some information on player type [07:18].
- Each play yields a pressure probability, not only a yes or no [07:48].
- Pressure is treated as the process that leads to sacks. PFF pressure rate and expected pressure rate together predict sack rate better than either alone, and tracking data also adds power when predicting a player's own pressure rate [08:19, 08:49].
- Expected pressure rate tracks combine and pro-day athleticism measures better than charted data does, which gives a time-varying athleticism measure in place of one combine number [09:19, 09:50].
- Coverage grades are unstable year to year. Linebacker "bite distance under expected" (BDU), the vertical displacement on play action adjusted for situation, is more predictive year to year than the coverage grade [10:20, 11:22, 12:23].
- Eager's reasoning for BDU: biting on a fake leaves the middle of the field open, the most valuable area to throw [10:51, 11:22].
- A receiver model using mean, median and max speed over a play found speed to be the most important variable for a positive PFF grade on go and corner routes [13:25, 13:55].
- The resulting speed-adjusted grade is steadier year to year than the deep-pass grade and correlates with the 40-yard dash, with exceptions such as Landry (slow 40, good receiver) and Kupp (faster on field than his timed run) [13:55, 14:25, 14:56].
- Tracking data's promise may not be reached without combining it with charting and play-by-play [15:27].

## Numbers and definitions

- Sacks take about two points on average from an offense [05:45].
- Sack rate predicting itself year to year: about 0.24 (R squared), given with "I think" and "or something" [08:19].
- BDU is described as three or four times more predictive year to year (R squared) than the coverage grade. The captions read "about four times three or four times", so the exact multiple is garbled [11:53, 12:23].
- Kupp's pro-day 40 time: 4.62 (caption "cooper cup"; the speaker was unsure of the year and said 2017) [14:56].
- Pressure: charted when a rusher moves the quarterback off his spot or gets a sack. Win rate: charted as whether the rusher won the rep. The two are correlated but can differ [05:15, 05:45].
- PFF grades are discrete steps of half a point from negative two (caption wording) [26:36].
- First-second speed was measured in the vertical (y) direction and as straight-line distance [06:47].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Charted grades as labels, tracking features as predictors (pressure, win rate, receiver grade) [06:16, 13:25].
- XGBoost classification for pressure [06:47].
- Adjusting linebacker displacement for situation (run tendencies, down and distance) and averaging over time [11:22, 11:53].
- Year-to-year R squared as the test of whether a new measure is better than the existing grade [08:19, 12:23].

## Limits and open questions

- The slides are not visible. Most R squared values, sample sizes, seasons and the number of plays are not in the captions, so only the 0.24 and the "three or four times" claims can be quoted.
- The speaker works for PFF and presents PFF tools as results, so this is an institutional and commercial view.
- The 40-yard dash question (correlation of about 0.75 raised by a questioner) concerns career averages versus one-time combine results, not within-player prediction, and the exchange is partly unclear [22:31, 23:31].
- Eager agreed in Q&A that BDU says nothing alone about whether a defender's passivity is worth what it costs against the run [18:58, 19:28].
- The linebacker examples are individual cases (Warner, Kuechly, Hewitt, Cunningham, White, David as heard in the captions); no group-level validation is shown beyond the R squared claim [11:53, 18:58, 24:31].
- Names in the captions may be misspelled (Kuechly appears as "luke lee"; Okereke as "okariki").

## Q&A

- An economist-style questioner asked about second-order effects (tired linemen, scheme and play-calling changes). Eager agreed, noting football has many columns but few rows, and that the game changes quickly, with play action as an example [16:28, 16:58, 17:28].
- Is the linebacker metric the right objective, since it measures the mean rather than variance? Eager is studying the trade-off (a good run defender may accept some middle-field plays) and wants analytics to quantify it [18:28, 18:58, 19:28].
- Do the receiver rankings match popular opinion? Eager discussed Tyreek Hill and Antonio Brown (caption spelling "tyree kill") and argued the measure captures controlled speed usable for football plays [20:28, 20:59, 21:30].
- Clarifying the 40-yard R squared table: it uses careers, because players test only once [22:31, 23:01, 23:31].
- Do defensive backs or linebackers who cushion create bias? Eager suggested team-level view of the two inside linebackers, because one may bite while the other covers [24:01, 24:31, 25:02].
- Why do context variables such as yards to go matter in the grade model? PFF does not ask graders to do context math, and the model partly adjusts for it [26:03, 26:36, 27:07].

# Applications: Using Tracking and Charting Data to Better Evaluate NFL Players (SSAC22)

## Where this applies

- Inference: Wide receiver speed in context. Eager contextualized in-game speed (mean, median, max over a play) against PFF grades on go and corner routes [13:25, 13:55]. Baylor already holds Catapult max velocity per session and PFF grades. A first pass could line up each receiver's game max velocity with PFF receiving grades on vertical routes, to see who turns speed into graded plays and who does not.
- Inference: Test speed versus game speed in recruiting grading. Eager's Landry and Kupp examples show players whose on-field speed differs from their combine or pro-day time [14:25, 14:56]. For Baylor, a table of pro-day or camp 40 time next to in-season Catapult peak velocity would flag recruits and transfers whose game speed is not visible in the timed number.
- Inference: Stability check before trusting any new metric. Eager judged his new measures by how well they predicted the same player the next year, compared with the existing PFF grade [08:19, 12:23]. Baylor could apply the same year-to-year (or half-season to half-season) check to any GPS or force plate metric before it goes into a coach-facing report.
- Inference: Treat PFF grades as coarse ordinal data when correlating them with load or testing numbers. Eager said the grades come in half-point steps and that graders are not asked to do context math [26:36, 27:07]. Correlations between a grade and a Catapult or VALD variable should account for that coarseness and for down, distance and route context.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: Weekly tracking is preferred over infrequent testing so plateaus and declines are caught early (Inferred, course material). The talk extends this: Eager argues a single combine measurement is a poor lifetime label for an athlete and that on-field data gives a time-varying version [09:19, 14:56]. Agrees in direction.
- Eric's baseline: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention," and a test that cannot be collected consistently is bad data (Explicit). The talk is consistent with this only in a limited way. It adds value by reusing data the team already collects (Catapult, PFF) rather than adding a test.
- Eric's baseline: No sport-specific or position-specific GPS thresholds exist in the documented data dictionary, and building them is named as unfinished work (Explicit, gap). The talk's situation adjustment for play action (down, distance, run tendency) [11:22, 11:53] is an example of the contextualizing that gap implies. Extends.

## What would have to be true

- Per-play or per-rep tagging in Catapult so that peak speed on a specific route or rush can be pulled, not just whole-session peaks.
- Enough games and targets per player for a stable estimate. Eager showed career averages and multi-year stability, not single-game values. The talk does not state how many plays were needed.
- PFF grades and Catapult data matched by player, play and date without manual rework.
- Agreement that "speed" means peak or mean velocity over the same window in both sources.

## Do not apply when

- The data is a college sample from one team. Eager's tracking source is league-wide shoulder-pad RFID [02:40]; Baylor sees only its own sensors, with no opponent comparison group.
- Inference: A player has too few snaps, or only one season, so the year-to-year logic cannot be tested.
- Inference: A grade is used as ground truth when it is itself a judgment. Eager's own response to a question was that the grade model partly refines coarse grading [26:36, 27:07]; it does not remove grader judgment.
- Inference: The result is used to rank defenders on play-action behavior without scheme context. Eager himself noted in Q&A that one linebacker may bite while his partner covers [24:31, 25:02].
- The 0.75 figure raised in Q&A is attached to career averages versus combine results [23:31]; do not treat it as a within-player prediction.

## First step

Inference: For one position group (receivers), list each player's best 40 time and their top in-game Catapult velocity from last season in one sheet, next to their PFF receiving grade on go or corner routes. Look at it, do not model it, and note which players stand out in either direction.

## Summary

ESPN analytics staff walk through how they built Receiver Tracking Metrics from NFL Next Gen Stats tracking data. The metric has three parts: open score, catch score and yards after catch, combined into an overall score on a 0 to 99 scale. They also trace the earlier history, including pass rush and pass block win rates, coverage and route classification models, and the problems of crediting receivers when they create their own context, accounting for the quarterback, and combining mixed units. The audience Q&A covers missing data, scheme, predictiveness and defender metrics. The stated goal is fan engagement, not team use.

## Key claims

- ESPN's analytics aim to tell stories and engage fans, not to help a team win [02:03].
- The receiver metric has open, catch and yards-after-catch components [04:06].
- Open score is more than distance to the nearest defender; it uses orientation, speed and trajectory, credits untargeted receivers, and looks 0.2 seconds before release [06:12], [08:19], [08:50], [09:21].
- Tracking access began in 2017, and it took almost half a season just to understand the data [11:24].
- A closest-defender script revealed who blocks whom, leading to pass rush and pass block win rates [14:59].
- On the first win-rate check, Joe Thomas ranked low on sacks allowed but third on pass block win rate, explained by the quarterback holding the ball [16:02], [16:34].
- Coverage and route classification models were built first and became components of the receiver metric [19:39], [20:41].
- Catch score uses a position-invariant convolutional neural network to estimate catch probability and credits catches over prediction [23:47], [24:17].
- The problem that receivers create their own context was solved by combining general and specific context estimates, benchmarked against a simple model [25:18], [25:49], [26:20], [26:52].
- Yards after catch uses the dots at the catch plus video-tracked ball placement [28:23], [28:55].
- The quarterback affects open score; Mahomes was average on catch score but very high on open score [29:55], [30:27].
- Seattle's receivers rated highly and Denver's lowest, which could partly explain Wilson's decline; the speakers hedge this [33:59], [34:32], [35:02].
- Component weights vary by position and were set by correlation with yards per route run [36:32], [37:03].
- Rookie receivers Olave, Wilson, Pickens and Watson ranked in the top 21; Olave in the top 10 [38:04], [38:34].
- Results are public via 538 [40:06]; the 0 to 99 scale was chosen for fan readability and the yards-after-catch scale was clipped [42:44], [43:15].
- A defender version failed because blame is unclear, especially in zone coverage [44:15].
- Open score is the most stable year to year, about as consistent as batting average, with catch and yards after catch behind; whether it predicts outcomes is still undetermined [53:28], [54:59].

## Numbers and definitions

- AJ Brown score 86, five points above the next player (Travis Kelce, caption "Kelsey") midseason [03:05].
- Release window: 0.2 seconds before release [08:50].
- Speed examples: 4.6 versus 10.3 miles per hour; 9 versus 13 [08:19], [09:21].
- Metric launched October 2022 after a six-year journey [10:23].
- Win rate: share of plays a player sustains or beats a block for 2.5 seconds [41:43].
- Catch example: 0.75 predicted probability, residual of 0.25 credited on a catch [24:17].
- Score scale: 0 to 99; Debo Samuel's yards-after-catch season would be the 99 and the next best about 60 [43:15].
- Joe Thomas: 53rd (speaker unsure whether sacks or pressures) versus third in pass block win rate [16:02].
- Orlando Brown 16th or 18th in pass block win rate [48:49].
- The "30 of the ESPN analytics team" figure is unclear in captions [01:03].

## Methods and frameworks named

- NFL Next Gen Stats tracking data (x and y only) plus ESPN video charting [11:24], [46:15].
- Position-invariant convolutional neural network [23:47].
- Expected versus predicted catch probability, combined [26:52].
- Adjusted plus-minus across seasons for quarterback and receiver effects [29:55].
- Weighting components by correlation with yards per route run [37:03].
- Year-to-year player-level correlation to test stability [54:29].

## Limits and open questions

- Predictiveness is not established; stability is stated qualitatively, with a self-correction on order of catch and yards after catch [54:59].
- No z-axis, no game-leverage context, no progression data [46:15], [47:18], [45:15].
- Scheme and quarterback cannot be separated [51:55].
- Presented by the metric's builders; ESPN's content purpose is stated [02:03].
- Garbled caption names: Diggs, Kelsey, Michael Horton, Dantzler, and the quarterback named after Joe Thomas [04:37], [16:34], [23:47].

## Q&A

- Wanted data: quarterback progression [45:15].
- Z-axis: not available [46:15].
- Time and score context: not included [47:18].
- Teammate influence: gravity credit for double teams [47:49].
- Yards after catch context: dots and blockers [50:20].
- Scheme versus quarterback: cannot be separated [51:55].
- Predictiveness: still to be determined [53:28].
- Win rate to sacks: predictive, with a finishing skill separate [55:29].
- Route types: should be accounted for; go routes inefficient, crossing and out routes efficient [57:32].

# Applications: SSAC23 Creating an NFL Player Tracking Metric (ESPN)

## Where this applies

- Inference: Recruiting grading for receivers and backs. The talk splits a receiver into getting open, making the catch and yards after the catch, each scored separately [22:14]. A Baylor grading sheet could carry three separate sub-grades for a prospect instead of one number, using PFF grades and film, so staff can see which skill is strong.
- Inference: The speaker's habit of building a much simpler benchmark model to check whether a complex model adds anything [25:49] applies to any internal metric Eric builds from GPS or force plate data. The concrete step is to compare a new composite readiness or load score against a simple baseline (a single raw metric) before presenting it.
- Inference: The point that a metric should be tested for year-to-year stability at the player level [54:29] maps to Eric's monitoring metrics. For each GPS or VALD variable, compute the correlation of an athlete's value across seasons or blocks and favor the stable ones for talent assessment, and the volatile ones for day-to-day monitoring only.
- Inference: Naming a metric for what it literally measures, not as a grade [41:43], is a presentation rule for coach-facing reports: label a number as "percent of reps above a speed threshold", not "speed grade".
- Inference: Mixed-unit composite scores needed conversion to a common scale and a weighting rule [36:32]. Any Baylor composite (for example a readiness index across jump and GPS variables) faces the same problem and could use the same rule: weight each component by how well it relates to an accepted outcome measure.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: Force plate reporting follows an output, driver and strategy framework (adopted from Hawkin Dynamics), with extra metrics added only for a defensible reason. The talk's three-part split (open, catch, yards after the catch) is a similar way of separating skills, though it concerns a receiver's play rather than a jump test. It extends the idea but does not describe the same framework.
- Eric's baseline: Data collection is judged on cost versus insight, and inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data. The talk's stability check [54:29] agrees in spirit, as a way to test whether a metric holds up before relying on it.
- Eric's baseline: A small number of valid, reliable tests is favored over an exhaustive battery (course-team position, speaker unconfirmed, Inferred). The talk builds a composite from three components and then weights them; it does not say fewer is better, so it is neutral here.
- No direct link found for Baylor's PFF-based recruiting grading process; the baseline document does not describe it.

## What would have to be true

- Tracking-based metrics need tracking data. The talk's metric rests on league-provided player tracking and ESPN video charting [28:55]. Baylor would need equivalent positional data (GPS positions in practice, or charted film) to build anything similar, and this talk does not show that college data of that kind exists in volume.
- A metric benchmarked against yards per route run [37:03] needs a trusted outcome measure. Eric would need a comparable accepted outcome for his own use case.
- The stability result (open score about as consistent as batting averages [54:59]) is the speakers' statement, so it would need a Baylor-side check.

## Do not apply when

- The scoring is used to rank NFL receivers for fans. ESPN's stated goal is to engage and entertain fans, not to win games [02:03]; the speakers state they would build a different final number for a team [42:44].
- Sample sizes are small, such as a single college season for a prospect, with a changing quarterback and scheme. The speakers admit scheme and quarterback effects are hard to separate and are largely unaccounted for [51:55].
- The decision depends on situational pressure. The speakers state the metric ignores game leverage [47:18].
- Predictive claims are needed. The speakers say that predictiveness is still unknown [53:28].

## First step

Take one GPS or force plate variable Eric already tracks for football and compute its correlation across two consecutive seasons for athletes who appear in both. Record the result next to the metric's definition, as a first stability note.

# Prediction Is Not Attribution in Defensive Evaluation

**What it is** — Ben Jenkins (PhD candidate at Florida Atlantic University, as he introduces himself) argues that football has a "defensive attribution problem" (JHgeEo3n1do [00:00]). On a running play tackled for a 6-yard loss, traditional metrics credit only the tackler, though several defenders contributed (JHgeEo3n1do [00:00], [00:31]). He contrasts two model types. A supervised model asks what will happen, is correlation-based, minimizes prediction error, and in his words "often confuses correlation with causation," is biased toward high-volume tacklers, and struggles to separate skill from opportunity (JHgeEo3n1do [01:01], [01:31]). A causal model asks what would happen if the defender had not made the tackle, which he says isolates individual contributions, accounts for situational context, and separates player effect from team and scheme effects (JHgeEo3n1do [01:31], [02:01]). His bottom line: "prediction is different than attribution" (JHgeEo3n1do [02:01]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives one reason for the contrast: a predictive model optimizes error loss, not an estimate of one player's contribution (JHgeEo3n1do [02:01]). He gives no further mechanism for why high-volume tacklers are favored. Inference: a defender who is often near the ball will correlate with good outcomes whether or not he caused them, and a loss function that only rewards prediction accuracy has no reason to separate the two.

**When to apply** — When a number is going to be read as "this player caused this result" (contract, grade, or scheme decisions, which the speaker lists as uses at JHgeEo3n1do [10:11]) and the underlying model was fit only to predict an outcome. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q12) says ACWR is "raw, has error, is misleading, and lacks context generally" (Explicit). Inference: that is the same worry, a summary number read as if it explained something. Ask of any Baylor metric whether it was built to predict or to attribute.

**When NOT to apply** — The speaker himself lists the limits of the causal side: it "requires a larger set of assumptions," needs more quality control, and cannot be applied in every scenario (JHgeEo3n1do [02:01]). The comparison with supervised models is his own; no head-to-head numbers appear in the captions beyond "better correlation" with honors (JHgeEo3n1do [07:39]). The data are NFL tracking data (the speaker names the 2024 NFL Big Data Bowl, JHgeEo3n1do [00:31]) for the first 9 weeks of the 2022 regular season, and he calls the work a proof of concept (JHgeEo3n1do [09:10]). It is an assertion from a competition presentation, not a validated finding, hence `untested`. It does not transfer to college or Baylor data without a tracking source.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the 6-yard-loss run, where the tackler gets the credit and, in his model, four other defenders also receive positive value (JHgeEo3n1do [06:08]). See [[case-study--one-play-and-aaron-donald-expected-points-saved]].

**Related** — [[framework--expected-points-saved-treatment-outcome-and-propensity-weighting]] — the model built on this premise. [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]] — a library framework on separating raw output from its interpretation. [[framework--receiver-creates-own-context-general-plus-specific-estimates]] — the ESPN talk faces a similar credit problem for receivers (teg9SfzpMy0 [25:18]); a panelist there says the nearest-defender version of defender credit "just isn't immediately clear" in zone coverage (teg9SfzpMy0 [44:15]).

# Expected Points Saved: Tackle as Treatment, EPA as Outcome, Propensity Weighting

**What it is** — The speaker, Ben Jenkins, frames defender credit as a treatment effect (JHgeEo3n1do [04:02]).
- **Treatment:** a binary indicator that the defender made the tackle on the play.
- **Outcome:** expected points added (EPA), the traditional NFL metric of how much the offense benefits.
- **Expected points saved (EPS):** expected EPA on the play if the defender did not make the tackle, minus expected EPA if he did (JHgeEo3n1do [04:02], [04:33]).
- **Architecture:** a transformer that processes all 22 players at once; the speaker says its attention mechanism captures defender coordination and interference effects (JHgeEo3n1do [04:33]).
- **Inputs (shown on a causal graph, DAG):** each defender's x-y position, speed and direction; the same for the ball carrier; relational features (defender relative to ball carrier); the 10 teammates of each defender; opponents; game context (JHgeEo3n1do [04:33], [05:04]).
- **Two models:** a propensity score model (probability a defender makes a tackle given all tracking information) and an outcome model (expected EPA with and without that defender's tackle) (JHgeEo3n1do [05:04], [05:35]).
- **Weighting:** inverse propensity weighting to build a "pseudo population" in which tackle involvement is independent of context and "effectively randomized" (JHgeEo3n1do [05:35]).
- **Doubly robust estimation:** named at the close as protection "against model misspecification" (JHgeEo3n1do [09:41]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's stated logic is that reweighting by the inverse of the probability of being involved removes the context that made involvement likely (JHgeEo3n1do [05:35]), and a low-probability defender who makes a tackle gets higher weight (JHgeEo3n1do [12:13]). He gives no proof or diagnostic that the propensity model balances the groups. Inference: the estimate is only as good as the propensity model, which the talk does not show being checked.

**When to apply** — As a recipe for any "who deserves credit" question where several people act on one outcome: define the treatment, define the outcome, model who gets the treatment, then reweight. Eric's baseline: none found. method-baseline.md holds no position on causal inference or counterfactual models. Inference: Baylor lacks league-wide tracking data for this exact build, so the lasting use is the design logic (treatment, outcome, propensity, weighting) when judging an outside metric someone brings to Applied Performance.

**When NOT to apply** — The speaker calls it a proof of concept on the first 9 weeks of the 2022 NFL regular season (JHgeEo3n1do [09:10]). The captions do not say how many plays per defender, how the propensity model was checked, or how the "treatment" is defined for players who get credit without tackling (JHgeEo3n1do [06:08]). The video description names adversarial representation balancing, Bayesian uncertainty and sensitivity analyses, but none is described in the talk (JHgeEo3n1do meta.json description, not in the talk). Scheme and assignment are not in the data (JHgeEo3n1do [11:43]). `untested`: no validation values are given in the captions.

**Example** — The speaker's example play: the tackler scores highest and four other defenders get positive value (JHgeEo3n1do [06:08]). See [[case-study--one-play-and-aaron-donald-expected-points-saved]].
